title: Strong Sense of Identity Linked to Mental Well-Being
paragraphs: Although many people believe we figure out who we are as teenagers or young adults, new research suggests that identity development continues throughout our adult lives — and that it could have a significant impact on our mental well-being.

Researchers in Finland looked at data from a study that has been following the same group of people since 1968. The participants — 196 boys and 173 girls — came from a town in central Finland, and were about 8 years old when the study began.

The researchers looked at data from surveys and interviews done when the participants were aged 27, 36, 42, 50 and 61. Each time, participants were asked to explain their political opinions and religious beliefs, as well as things like their expectations in a relationship, the type of lifestyle that appealed to them, and their sense of what their career was.
The researchers wanted to know whether participants had considered different beliefs and choices in these areas, and whether they had made firm decisions about what they believed or wanted.
Based on their answers, the researchers assessed how far each participant had progressed in developing their identity across these different areas of life.

The results showed that people's identities continue to develop well into middle age and later years, with the most rapid identity growth happening between ages 27 and 42 — suggesting that this may be a particularly important period for identity development.
Although people's identities continue to develop after age 42, it's at a much slower rate.

Looking at participants' mental health over the years, the data showed that people with a better developed identity enjoy higher levels of mental well-being and life satisfaction, with fewer anxious feelings and stronger social connections.
However, the researchers also noted that, while a strong identity may support mental well-being, the opposite could also be true, with mental well-being supporting the formation of a strong identity.
